title: Scientists discover a previously unknown mineral inside a 5,000-year-old Polish meteorite and name it copernikite after astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus
byline: TOI Science Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Nov 07, 2026, 01:00 IST

content:
PC: University of Silesia / National Geographic

A meteorite that landed in what is now Poland thousands of years ago has yielded another discovery, with scientists identifying a mineral that had not previously been formally recognised.

As reported by the University of Silesia, the material was found inside the Morasko meteorite, an iron-rich space rock that fell near Poznań between 5,000 and 6,000 years ago. Given the name copernikite, the mineral honours Nicolaus Copernicus, the Polish astronomer whose work changed how people understood the Solar System. Its identification adds to a growing list of minerals associated with the meteorite and brings the total number of new minerals discovered by scientists at the University of Silesia to 80.

How Copernicus inspired the name of the newly recognised mineral

The discovery was formally accepted in early 2026 by the Commission on New Minerals, Nomenclature and Classification of the International Mineralogical Association (CNMNC-IMA). The mineral has the chemical formula K(Ti₇Cr)O₁₆ and was assigned the name copernikite in recognition of Copernicus, who lived between 1473 and 1543.Although the material itself was previously unfamiliar as a formally established mineral, compounds with a broadly similar composition had appeared in scientific literature decades earlier.

Reportedly, comparable phases were identified in Australian lamproites in 1982, rocks associated with diamond deposits. However, those earlier findings were not accompanied by the detailed investigation needed to establish the material as a distinct mineral species.

Where scientists found copernikite inside the Morasko meteorite

The mineral was located in a particularly complex part of the Morasko meteorite. Its metallic material contains rounded to oval nodules made up of troilite and graphite, with different mineral combinations occurring inside them.

Some of these nodules measure several centimetres across, providing scientists with small but varied environments to investigate.Copernikite was identified in just one specimen examined by the research team. The individual grains were extremely small, reaching no more than 0.3 millimetres. They occurred within fluorapatite in a graphite-rich area containing troilite inclusions.Its appearance also offered a clue to its composition. Chromium is responsible for the mineral's green colour, although the grains shown in the published microscopic image appear light grey under reflected light.The team also established that copernikite belongs to the priderite group, a family of minerals characterised by a structure containing channels or tunnels. Its arrangement of atoms places it among minerals with a hollandite-type tunnel structure. According to the University of Silesia, copernikite is the first oxide mineral with a tunnelled hollandite structure to have been identified in a meteorite anywhere in the world.

Why the mineral's tunnel structure matters

The internal arrangement of copernikite is different from the simple image many people might have of a mineral as a solid, uniform crystal. Its structure is built around octahedra containing titanium and chromium. These units connect to form the walls of channels, with potassium, barium and calcium occupying spaces within the tunnel-like arrangement.Understanding this architecture helps distinguish copernikite from other mineral phases with similar chemical ingredients.

Two materials can contain comparable elements but still have different atomic arrangements, making their crystal structures an important part of determining whether they represent separate mineral species.

Morasko meteorite has produced several new minerals

Copernikite is not the first mineral to emerge from investigations of the Morasko meteorite. It is the fourth new mineral species formally associated with the material.The earlier discoveries include moraskoite, described in 2015, followed by czochralskiite in 2016.

Crisaite was identified in 2025. The latest addition came from continued examination of the meteorite's nodules, which contain different mineral assemblages and have provided researchers with several opportunities to identify previously unrecognised substances.The meteorite takes its name from Morasko, a district in Poznań, western Poland, where fragments were found. Its fall to Earth is estimated to have occurred around five to six millennia ago.

Although it has been known for years, its mineral composition is still being investigated.

The research team behind the discovery

The investigation brought together specialists from several Polish scientific institutions. Professors Evgeny Galuskin and Irina Galuskina, from the Faculty of Natural Sciences at the University of Silesia, were among the researchers involved.They worked alongside Professor Andrzej Muszyński of Adam Mickiewicz University, as well as Professor Joachim Kusz and Dr Maria Książek from the University of Silesia's Faculty of Science and Technology. Grzegorz Zieliński, from the Polish Geological Institute – National Research Institute, also contributed to the work.
